en: The Diamond Sutra: Thus Spoken Meaning, Volume One.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
the nature of gold (*vajra*) is firm and hard, capable of shattering all things; likewise, when a person possesses wisdom, they are able to sever greed, hatred, and delusion.

All characteristics are, in the Sanskrit language, *prajñā*, and in the Chinese language, "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). Its essential nature is luminous and penetrating, skillfully destroying all afflictions and transforming them into sublime function.
In the Sanskrit language, it is *pāramitā*, and in the Chinese language, "reaching the other shore.

The realm where sentient beings perform actions, undergo suffering, and transmigrate through birth and death is called "this shore. The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas... [have thoroughly investigated] this.
Ultimately transcending to the ground of purity and bliss is called the "other shore" (*pāra*). Ordinary beings are this shore; the Buddha-way is the other shore.
A single thought of evil is this shore; a single thought of goodness is the other shore. The six realms of existence are like a sea of suffering;
without a boat, one cannot cross. Taking the six perfections of *prajñā* as a vessel, one crosses over the six realms.

The ocean of suffering; therefore, it is called "reaching the other shore. It is said that a person’s wisdom is as adamantine as gold, enabling them to be liberated from karmic obstructions and attain the stage of Buddhahood; hence, it is called the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This is the direct path—the shortcut for studying the Buddha and the road to attaining Buddhahood. If ordinary people wish to reach this path, they should cultivate *prajñā* within.

Whether one reaches the ultimate consummation or merely recites and explains the text without the mind following its practice, such a person seeks the Buddha outside the body and seeks the sutras outwardly;
they will ultimately fail to awaken to principle or see their nature. Therefore, the Buddha named this the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
its essential purpose is to lead people from the state of an ordinary being to the realization of sagehood, so that the deluded mind may forever cease.
Section One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly. This marks the beginning of the discourse and the gathering. "Section" (fen) means a division.
Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty divided the text into thirty-two sections because the scriptural passages were so vast, so as to make them convenient for lecturing and recitation.
Thus have I heard.
Ānanda himself declared that these teachings were heard by him from the Buddha, thereby clarifying that they were not his own composition.

"Thus" (evam) refers to the nature of sentient beings, which is manifold in its myriad distinctions; their movements and stillnesss vary, such that nothing can be used for comparison and no two are equal.
"This" refers precisely to the nature of sentient beings; apart from this nature, there is no other dharma. That dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*);
that all are the Buddha-dharma is called "This. "Hearing" means listening. Listening is not a state of no-hearing, nor is it a state of having hearing;
to be completely free from grasping or rejecting is called "true hearing. Therefore it is said: "Water does not depart from the waves; the waves are [the water]."
Water. When the mirror-water is untouched by dust or wind, it manifests without flaw, reflecting heaven and earth. Again, a verse says: The monkey cries upon the ridge;
The crane calls amidst the forest. Severed clouds are swept away by the wind; Water dashes through the long rapids.
I love most the deep night of late autumn frost, When the cry of a single wild goose awakens one to the cold of heaven.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍika Park.
"At one time" refers to the specific occasion when he preached the Dharma. "Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the language of China (Huayan), it means "Awakened.

This signifies that he is able to awaken to his own nature and, simultaneously, to awaken all sentient beings. Confucius said: "In the West, there is a Great Sage who does not govern... [The text continues].
Yet he was not disordered; he inspired confidence without speaking, and his practice proceeded without being exhorted. This specifically refers to the Buddha.
He was born during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty and was named Śākya. Śrāvastī is the country where King Prasenajit resided.
Jetavana is the grove bestowed by Jeta, the crown prince of King Prasenajit. There was a man named Sudatta in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He constantly gave alms to the solitary and the poor, and for this reason he was called the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.

Once, he went to the house of the Elder Jeta to seek a marriage alliance. That family had invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma; upon hearing of this, Sudatta’s mind was opened and his understanding awakened.

He wished to invite the Buddha back home, so the Buddha instructed him to return first and seek a site for the monastery. There was only the garden belonging to Prince Jeta, so he went there to request it.
The Crown Prince said in jest, "If you spread gold to fill the garden, I shall grant it to you. Sudatta then proceeded to transport and spread the gold.
Seeing his sincerity, the Crown Prince withdrew the gold and granted him the land, and they together constructed a vihāra and invited the Buddha to preach the Dharma;
therefore, it was named the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden. The Buddha was about to preach a sūtra while staying there.
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
In the Sanskrit language, *bhikṣu* means: *bhi* signifies "to destroy," and *kṣu* signifies "afflictions" (*kleśa*). It refers to one who is able to destroy and eliminate afflictions.

In the Chinese language, it is translated as *seng* (monk), and is also called *qishi* (alms-seeker). [The alms-seeker] seeks the Dharma from the Buddhas above to clarify their own true nature; below, they seek...
He ate with the people of the world so as to enable them to plant seeds of merit. As for the great bhikṣus, they were those who had attained the profound depths of the Way.

When the Buddha wished to expound the wondrous principle of true emptiness and formlessness, how could anyone but a great bhikṣu of accomplished talent and realized virtue achieve sudden enlightenment upon hearing his words?
Therefore, he dwelt together with them in the garden; his assembly numbered one thousand two hundred.
Fifty people were fully present, seeing and following with faith in great numbers.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and having gone through the streets begging for food in order, returned to his original place.
At that time—meaning at that particular occasion—the Buddha was the Honored One of the three realms, revered by the entire world; thus he was called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*).
While in the midst of eating his meal, he donned the garment of gentle forbearance and, holding the alms-bowl offered by the Four Heavenly Kings, went among the people to beg for food.
Although the Buddha had been a prince, he nevertheless held the bowl and begged for alms, desiring to...
Monks of future generations shall not accumulate assets nor give rise to thoughts of arrogance.

As those who beg in successive order, they shall not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy or the noble and the lowly, but shall go from door to door to beg with great compassion and equanimity; having finished their begging, they shall return to the monastery grounds.
Having finished eating, he gathered his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and sat down upon a prepared seat.
Upon completing the meal, he gathered his robes and bowl without any lingering attachment; he washed his feet for the sake of purity; and he spread out a seat as an arrangement for the lecture.
This is the standard procedure for preaching the Dharma. Master Zhizhe composed a verse on this: "The Dharma-body is fundamentally not food."
The manifestations of transformation are likewise so: to increase the merit of humans and devas, he acts as a field of blessings through his compassion.

Having gathered his robes and stilled his labors and anxieties, he washes his feet to distance himself from worldly conditions. Desiring to realize the principle of the three voids, he sits cross-legged and demonstrates entry into dhyāna.
Chapter Two: The Section on the Request by Subhūti. Subhūti is an alternative name for Śāriputra. At the time of his birth, his entire household became empty;
an astrologer divined his fate and found it to be entirely auspicious and virtuous, hence he was also named Śubhagata (The Auspicious One).
Rising from within the great assembly, he requested instruction on the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti, rising from his seat amidst the great assembly—[omitting "至" (zhì) as it indicates an ellipsis]—addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is rare, World-Honored One.
The term "Elder" (*sthavira*) denotes one of high virtue and venerable age. He rose from his seat intending to request the Buddha to preach the Dharma;
he bared his right shoulder, which is the etiquette for performing service and labor, and the ritual for repenting and apologizing for transgressions. He placed his right knee upon [the ground].
The ground: the right is the correct path, and the left is the deviant path. This refers to taking refuge by means of the correct path.
With palms joined, the mind merges with the Path, and the Path merges with the mind; thus, one withdraws and arouses reverence, entirely regulating one’s deportment to present these words of inquiry.
"Rare indeed" praises the Buddha as one seldom seen in all the world.
"The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
This passage consists of Subhūti’s words of inquiry; therein he first addresses the Buddha as "Tathāgata. As for "Tathā" (Thus):
"Quiescent and unmoving" is the fundamental essence of true nature (*tathatā*). "Coming forth" refers to its application, which responds to stimuli and thereby penetrates all things.
The mind is ever empty and still, profoundly pure; it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. For this reason, a Buddha is called a *Tathāgata* (Thus-Come One).
As for "skillfully protecting and mindful[ly caring]": it means to cause all students to use the wisdom of *prajñā* to refine themselves.
He does not allow his body and mind to give rise to false hatred or attachment, thereby becoming defiled by the six sense objects and falling into the ocean of suffering of birth and death;

it is solely because he skillfully protects and mindfuly cares for them, and further skillfully entrusts and charges the various Bodhisattvas, instructing them to uphold the Dharma and act accordingly.

"Be diligent in every thought-moment; do not allow it to be interrupted. Subhūti spoke these two phrases desiring that the Buddha preach the Dharma to instruct people, so that they might realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
A bodhisattva is precisely one who receives the Tathāgata’s teaching.
This is a general designation for those who practice. Since there are many who occupy the seat of instruction, they are called "all bodhisattvas.
[The World-Honored One said: "Good sons and good daughters... how should they dwell? How should they subdue their minds?"
"Good son, it is the mind of right concentration. Good daughter, it is the mind of right wisdom.

This means that one is able to decisively resolve upon concentration and wisdom, never again falling back. *A* means 'non-existence'; it refers to the absence of all defilements. *Anuttara* means 'supreme'."
There is nothing in the three realms that can compare to it. "Three" refers to correctness; it is right view. "Miao" means pervasive;
there is not a single sentient being among all those who do not possess it pervasively. "Three Bodhi" means knowledge—knowledge that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
In Sanskrit, this is *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; in the language of China, it is translated as "Unsurpassed, Right, Equal, and Perfect Enlightenment. This means:
This is the true nature (*dharmatā*). One who attains this nature becomes a Buddha; they transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*) and no longer undergo cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) means to remain still without shifting. "Subduing" (*vinaya*) means being able to restrain and govern [the mind]. Subhūti then asked:
"If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the aspiration for perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), in what place should they [abide]?"
Abiding in peace. All sentient beings are restless and ceaseless, like dust motes stirred by a whirling wind;
moment after moment they succeed one another without interval. If one wishes to practice cultivation, by what path should one subdue the mind?
The Venerable One desired instruction on the method for practicing meditation. Master Chuan said, "From where does this question emerge?
He then offered this verse: "You find joy, but I do not; You feel sorrow, but I do not. The wild goose longs to fly north across the passes;
The swallow remembers its old nest and returns home. In the autumn moon and spring flowers lies boundless meaning— Within this, only you yourself may know."
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! [You have] well entrusted the bodhisattvas.
The Buddha praised what Subhūti had said: "The Tathāgata’s two phrases are most excellent. You are able to understand my intention;

you have skillfully instructed all people not to give rise to deluded thoughts, but to always maintain diligent effort in their minds, so that they do not become defiled by or attached to the characteristics of phenomena."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you... [up to] 'you should abide in this manner and thus subdue your mind.
'Attentively' means with thorough examination. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives rise to the mind of perfect enlightenment, that is the very place where one should rest;
one should abide therein and must not depart from it even for a moment. Should the deluded mind happen to stir, one should..."
This is the method for mastery. Both cases are thus: it is simply this very place; there is no need to seek elsewhere. The mind of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is active and deluded;
the mind of the sage (*ārya*) is still and luminous. Ordinary people are mostly hindered by circumstances obstructing the mind, and by phenomena obstructing principle.
They do not realize that because the mind is empty, circumstances are naturally empty; because principle is tranquil, phenomena are naturally tranquil. Mind and circumstance...
To forget both is the true Dharma. Forgetting objects is relatively easy; forgetting the mind is most difficult.
If one does not forget the mind but merely wishes to forget objects, the objects cannot be forgotten, and instead, confusion and turmoil increase. Therefore, all phenomena are but the mind.
If one can see one's nature and no longer give rise to deluded thoughts, this is precisely what it means to subdue the mind. Pang’s verse says: "The people of the world value treasures..."
“O Jewel, I value the stillness of a single kṣaṇa; gold, however, greatly disturbs the human mind. Through stillness, one perceives the nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
Indeed, World-Honored One, I wish most earnestly to hear this.
“Indeed” is a term of assent; Subhūti, having heard what the Buddha spoke, joyfully accepted it.
I pray that the Buddha will explain this extensively, so that those of middling and inferior capacities may all listen with joy and receive it, and that they may all attain awakening.
This is the third section, "The True Lineage of the Mahāyāna. It carries [the teaching] across; it carries across all sentient beings, and is thus the true and orthodox lineage.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way. 'Mahā' means great.
Although a mahāsattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they are truly one stage above ordinary bodhisattvas. The thoughts and reflections of such a bodhisattva are pure;
through the various skillful means of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, they transform and guide sentient beings. Mahā. Great.

Although the Bodhisattva dwells amidst the defilements of worldly toil, his mind remains ever pure; he and those he transforms are both free from attachment in their hearts, and thus he is a person of great enlightenment.
The delusive thoughts of the human mind most easily grow by stealth and in secret;
therefore, the Buddha told Subhūti and others, further emphasizing a single phrase: "One should subdue the mind in this manner. This means that one should employ this purity...

Wisdom is that which subdues the deluded mind. In the subsequent passage concerning the salvation of sentient beings, being without even a trace of attachment to signs is precisely the point where the mind is subdued.

All categories of sentient beings—up to those who are neither with perception nor without perception—all living creatures are called "sentient beings. They all possess Buddha-nature; it is not limited to humans alone.
Those born from eggs, such as birds; those born from wombs, such as humans and beasts; and those born from moisture, such as mosquitoes and fireflies.
They are born by transformation; they arise through metamorphosis, such as silkworms and moths. "Form" refers to the physical body; "perception" refers to thought and deliberation.
Those who possess form are submerged in emotional consciousness and the mind that clings to existence—those who falsely perceive right and wrong. As for those without form:
Those who have severed emotions and abandoned desire, yet cling to the mark of emptiness—those who do not cultivate merit and wisdom—are of two types.

Those with conceptual thought see with their eyes and hear with their ears, constantly giving rise to deluded thoughts; though they speak of the Buddha-dharma with their mouths, their minds do not accord with their practice.

Those without conceptual thought maintain stillness through seated meditation and are able to eliminate all deluded thoughts, becoming like wood or stone; yet they do not train in wisdom or skillful means. This is not [the way].
Regarding "neither with thought nor without thought": in a single moment, it is tranquil and unmoving; it appears as if there were no thought, yet in reality, within its emptiness, it can illuminate.
It is not that there is no thought. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside; speech and silence are both forgotten. There is no heart of grasping or rejecting, of love or hatred.
To enumerate the nine categories of beings one by one, this is precisely what is meant by "the minds of all sentient beings."
"I shall cause all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.
"I" refers to the Buddha speaking of himself. "Cause to enter" means to lead them to awakening and entry.

"Without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) means that one's meritorious practice is perfected, being pure and spontaneous, entirely free from habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and afflictions (*kleśa*). Within it, there is peace and bliss, with nothing further lacking, deficient, leaking, or fragmented.
Nirvana means the state of perfect purity. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Nirvana is pure; it is the realm where there is neither birth nor death.
It is that to which all practitioners turn for refuge. It is the transcendence of saṃsāra and the departure from birth and death;
it is the ultimate stage of the Tathāgata who has reached the other shore. As for "extinction" (*nirodha*), it refers to the total eradication of all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"Deliverance" means crossing over and being liberated from the ocean of suffering of birth and death. The Buddha says that all sentient beings are unable to become Buddhas because they are shrouded and fettered by deluded thoughts.

I shall cause them all to return together to awakening and reach the state of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, so that all sentient beings may receive transformation and deliverance, and all perceive the equality of the Buddha-mind. May I universally vow to [bring this about].
All sentient beings shall equally enter the perfect, pure, and remainderless nirvana; they shall together cross the ocean of suffering of birth and death;
and they shall share in that which all Buddhas have realized.
Thus, although I have brought immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa.
All sentient beings manifest from the conditions of their own karma:
some are born as humans, some are born in the heavens, some are born as animals, and some are born in the hells; none are born other than through the conditions of their own karma.

In reality, there are no such sentient beings. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Although I thus bring sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, it is truly because the original nature of sentient beings inherently possesses Buddhahood;
they were originally capable of saving themselves. It is only because they are unable to awaken that they are called 'sentient beings.
Even if one were to exhaustively deliver them—limitless, innumerable, and boundless—in this manner,"
Most [teachings] do not go beyond returning to one's original nature; how, then, can it be said that "I deliver others"? Therefore, it is said:
"In reality, there are no sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa. The *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* states: "To deliver oneself by means of one’s own nature is called true deliverance.
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The fundamental nature of all sentient beings is eternally extinguished; it does not undergo further extinction. Mañjuśrī—
The Bodhisattva asked the World-Honored One: "In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa; how is this so? The World-Honored One replied:
"Nature is fundamentally pure, without arising and without ceasing. Therefore, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa, nor is there any nirvāṇa to be reached."
All of these are attributed solely to the self-nature of sentient beings. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"If a person wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all is created by mind alone. A verse on the creation of phenomena through the mind states:

"The assignment of forms each arises from the mind; like shadows and echoes, there is no deception. Originally, there is no creator or artificer; it is the myriad living beings themselves [who create]."
The Transformation.
For what reason? Subhūti, [from this point] up to "the mark of a sentient being and the mark of a life-span are not the Bodhisattva," the Buddha addressed Subhūti and asked:
"For what reason does one deliver sentient beings? In reality, there is no one who can be delivered."
If a bodhisattva perceives that there are beings to be saved, they immediately awaken to this as a private calculation for themselves;
to boast of merit and display ability is an evil karma born of greed, which constitutes the mark of self (*ātman*). Where there is a self, there is a counterpart of others;

to discriminate between "you" and "I," or to weigh the wise against the foolish, is an evil karma born of anger, which constitutes the mark of persons (*pudgala*). Once one perceives the existence of persons, one cannot avoid making various kinds of distinctions.

The various categories of sentient beings give rise to emotional attachments toward whatever they encounter; being biased and clinging, these serve as the conditions for delusion and evil—this is the mark of a "sentient being" (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*).
Because there is the view of a person and the view of a sentient being, one refuses to be impartial and seeks only one's own welfare and benefit, calculating how to prolong one's life in the world;
this serves as the condition for craving and attachment—this is the mark of a "life-span" (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*). If these four types of characteristics exist, then I...
If the mind and wisdom are obscured by darkness, one remains on the same path of delusion as sentient beings and is no longer one who stands in the rank of a Bodhisattva.
This is why, although one delivers sentient beings, in reality there is no delivering.
To be able to eliminate the four marks [of self] is what is called "subduing the mind."
Chapter Four: On Sublime Practice Without Abiding. Sublime practice is fundamentally without abiding or attachment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices the Dharma, they should give in this manner: they should not abide in signs.
Subhūti originally rose from his seat to inquire; therefore, the Buddha commanded him to return to his place, so that by attaining stability, wisdom would arise.
The Buddha said, "The mind is devoid of the four marks. Where, then, does this mind dwell or cling?
It should be like clouds moving across the sky or water flowing over the earth, without any hindrance or obstruction. Whenever Master Jueyi saw a monk...
When someone came to ask a question, he simply held up a single finger. Chan Master Foguan composed a verse on this:
"No need to seek the mind outwardly; The message within has its source. To report the meaning of Bodhidharma’s coming from the West: It lies solely in the single finger of Kūṭi.
A Bodhisattva who has realized the emptiness of both person and phenomena possesses a mind free of grasping or rejection, and is thus able to know the holy.
In all things of one essence, emptiness and form are of the same nature; good and evil are of one rank.
Internally shatter all attachments and abide in non-abiding. Master Longji’s verse says: "When mind and objects are suddenly dissolved, only then does one clearly realize that form is emptiness.

If you wish to recognize your original face, look amidst the green mountains and white clouds. This is how one should dwell without attachment regarding the Buddha-dharma; it is not a matter of forced effort.
This is strength. Ordinary beings do not recognize their own Buddha-nature; they seek only outwardly, dwelling in appearances and deluding themselves regarding the truth.
They discriminate against external objects and cannot assist the Path, seeking only worldly benefits and rewards—like an arrow shot into the air, or like a person entering the darkness.
The Bodhisattva possesses this thought of non-abiding and practices giving. Whether it be forms and colors, sounds, fragrances, or flavors—
That which is touched by the emotions and that which is transformed and guided by the Dharma are called the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
All these are possessed in common by myself and all sentient beings. When one intends to practice giving, one does not perceive a self as the donor, nor does one perceive another as the recipient;
nor does one perceive any object in between to be given. Since these three entities are all devoid of defiled attachment, for this reason—
The nature of wisdom is to clearly perceive that all things are empty and to seek no karmic reward.
A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner alone, and must not dwell upon signs. Among the six perfections practiced by those on the path, giving is the foremost.
It is able to eliminate the afflictions and deluded thoughts of the four marks—self, person, sentient being, and life-span—as well as the mind that grasps and rejects or loves and hates.
One practices giving with purity, giving rise to no attachment; this is giving that does not dwell on marks. The verse by Fu says:

The river of dhyāna becomes still as the waves subside; the water of samādhi grows clear as the ripples cease. Clarity gives rise to the awakened nature; the loss of discursive thought extinguishes deluded sentiments.

Pervasive conceptualization is empty discrimination; from the beginning, names have been provisionally established. If one realizes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no separate perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit and virtue are inconceivable.
Why does a bodhisattva practice giving without dwelling on signs? It is because if a bodhisattva is thus non-abiding, they give whenever conditions arise and remain tranquil when conditions disperse;
their mind is pure, benefiting all beings. Although they do not seek blessings, they naturally [attain them].
They leave behind the suffering of birth and death and experience great bliss. Enduring for a thousand kalpas without aging, they transcend the three realms to remain forever in the present.
Their merit and virtue are self-attained, beyond thought and impossible to measure. Now, the Buddha prizes the signless (animitta).

For what reason is it said that one obtains merit? It is because [the Buddha], out of compassion for sentient beings who are defiled by and attached to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and cannot yet be transformed immediately, provisionally entices them with the boundlessness of merit and virtue.
"Subhūti, what do you think? [The passage continues] "...it is likewise thus and inconceivable.
"What do you think? Before the Buddha asks the question, he first instructs him to deliberate within his own mind.
"No, World-Honored One," Subhūti replies, indicating that it is not so. The Buddha then points to the four directions—east, south, west, and north—and the four intermediate points.
Throughout the ten directions, above and below, it is said that within the universe nothing is greater than empty space; it is inconceivable.

The merit obtained by a Bodhisattva through giving while remaining free from the mark of abiding fills all of empty space, and like the vastness of the ten directions, it cannot be measured or conceived.
Master Chuan said, "One may know the propriety of this. The verse says: The realm of empty space.
How could the realms be fathomed by thought? The Great Way is pure and serene, its principle even more vast.
As long as the wind and moon remain upon the Five Lakes, the spring breeze will continue to bring forth the fragrance of a hundred flowers.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
The Buddha called to Subhūti and said: "Regarding the place where this mind should rest, one should simply abide the mind according to the teaching on non-abiding in signs as explained above.
One must know that non-abiding in signs is itself subduing. If one can subdue it, the mind will then rest and not wander;
therefore, it is said that 'one should abide. The Samādhi Sūtra says: 'As for what the Tathāgata..."
He preached the Dharma entirely from the standpoint of non-abiding. From this place of non-abiding, I pay homage to the Tathāgata.
Although there are many words in the sutras, they all expound the wondrous principle of true emptiness and formlessness in order to transform and deliver sentient beings.
If sentient beings can abide in and subdue [the mind], such that the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span do not arise, they will then be able to reach the stage of Nirvana.
As for the teaching on giving, it is merely intended to make it easier for practitioners to enter the path;
originally, it is not considered particularly weighty. Once the great meaning of the sutra has been fully exhausted in this, the subsequent passages are nothing more than repetitions.
This section clarifies the meaning of signlessness (*animitta*), fearing that if people become attached to signs (*nimitta*), they will be unable to abide in and subdue [the mind].
Chapter Five:
"Discerning Reality as It Is" (*yathābhūta-darśana-vibhāga*). This is the true and authentic insight into the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
"Subhūti, what do you think? [This continues] until: "The so-called marks of the body are indeed no marks of the body.

The preceding passage spoke of abiding securely and subduing [the mind] to be able to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood; it was feared that people might suspect there is actually a Buddha-body visible to the eye.
Not knowing that there is a Tathāgata within their own minds, they asked Subhūti whether one could see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks.
Subhūti, having already understood the Buddha’s intention, replied, "No. The form-body (*rūpakāya*) possesses marks;

In Sanskrit this is called *sakṛdāgāmin*; in the language of China, it means "one who comes and goes once. This is the second fruit, which ranks one level higher than the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

One gradually cultivates the practice of diligence, maintaining a more refined discipline. Moment by moment, one does not dwell within the realms of the six sense objects; yet, one has still not fully attained purity.
It is merely that as soon as a preceding thought becomes attached, the succeeding thought immediately awakens to it; there remains [a trace of attachment].
This single instance of arising and ceasing is what is called "one coming and going.
Although the physical body has coming and going, the Dharma-body is serene and unmoving. Since the mind is without self, who can speak of coming and going?
It is merely designated as "one coming and going," yet in reality, there is no mind that attains this fruit of one coming and going. This is what is called a "false name."
The Sakṛdāgāmin. Fu’s Verse says: Having abandoned the state of ordinary beings and first entered the holy path, afflictions gradually become light and subtle.

Having severed the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, one for the first time realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding the perception of objects and the view of a self-body, only now does one know them to be false.
After returning once more to the realms of humans and devas, one hastens toward quiescence, no longer knowing how to return [to the world].
Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding the *anāgāmin*—[the text continues] "therefore he is called an *anāgāmin*.

In Sanskrit, *anāgāmin*; in the language of China, "one who does not come back. This is the third fruit. His cultivation and practice are even more profound than those of the person who has attained the second fruit.
The six sense objects no longer invade him at all; he has fully realized that both person and phenomena are empty. Having gradually cultivated with diligence...
Having severed the afflictions of desire within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one is reborn directly in the Tuṣita heaven palace and will never again return to be born in the realm of desire;

this is called attaining the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), and for this reason, one is named "Non-Returner" (*anāgāmin*). However, since the mind is empty and without self (*anātman*), what is there that does not return?
Therefore, it is called "Non-returning" (Anāgāmin); yet in reality, there is no mind that attains this fruit of non-returning.
Because in truth there is no such thing as non-returning, it is merely a provisional name for *anāgāmin*.

Master Chuanchan said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all are suffering. The verse says: The three stages of the Śrāvakas have already transcended the dust; having come and gone, they seek...
In stillness there is distance and intimacy; the four fruits of enlightenment are originally no fruit at all. This illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
Subhūti, what do you think? [From "Arhat" up to] "this is precisely attachment to self, person, sentient beings, and life-span."
In Sanskrit, *arhat*; in the language of China, "one who is without birth. Having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), they are free from further afflictions.
Having realized the principle of neither arising nor ceasing, this is the fourth fruit. It ranks one level higher than the three preceding fruits.
The Buddha said that when a practitioner reaches the stage of *arhat*, the Way is about to be attained; they themselves may also entertain this thought.
"And yet, they do not obtain it. Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Those who are called Arhats have already awakened to the principle of non-arising;
there are no afflictions to be severed, and no greed or hatred to be abandoned. Their emotions are neither adverse nor favorable, for both mind and objects are empty.
Thus, although they have attained the Way, their minds have never actually grasped a single dharma; they possess nothing more than a mere conventional name."

"O Arhat! If you entertain the thought, 'I have already attained the path of Arhatship,' you immediately become attached to the marks of self and personhood, thereby distancing yourself from the stage of an Arhat.
How then can you be called by that name? Regarding those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], it is said that they all lack a [discursive] mind.
Thus, one may see that the sages and worthies all rely on the unconditioned dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*) and do not dwell at all upon marks."

However, those who have attained only the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] realize this for themselves alone and do not save sentient beings; in the Buddha-dharma, these are called followers of the Hīnayāna.
The World-Honored One said: "I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention... I am an Arhat free from desire."
When defiled thoughts are about to arise, I intend to dispel them; when the two sides do not yield to one another, this is called "contention" (*raṇa*).

When the mind is without arising or ceasing, coming or going, and there is only the constant illumination of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), this is called "non-contention" (*araṇa*). This is precisely what constitutes liberation from human desires;

therefore, it is called an Arhat who has abandoned desire (*vītarāga-arhat*). *Samādhi* is a Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*). It is also called...

"Right reception" (samyaksamādhi) refers to the correctness of the method for entering meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), such that the objects experienced within that concentration are not products of deluded thought.
Subhūti said: "When I speak of those who have attained the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], they attain the fruit without a 'mind' (acittatā).

This is not a view based on my own fabrications; rather, it is according to my own experience. The Buddha once declared that I have attained the Way of Non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*), which is entirely..."
If one is as vast and empty as space and unattached, it is not merely being among those who possess samādhi; rather, one is foremost among those with samādhi.

This is the foremost Arhat, free from desire. Although the Buddha thus addressed me, I truly did not harbor the thought that I had attained this state of an Arhat free from desire. Master Chuanshan said: "If you grasp it firmly..."
Clouds hang across the mouth of the valley. To let go is for the moon to fall into the cold pool. The verse says: Calling it a horse, it was never a horse;
calling it an ox, it was not necessarily an ox. Letting both ends drop away, rest all at once in the middle way. A falcon from the vast heavens bursts forth from the six gates;
walking alone through heaven and earth, nothing is withheld.
“World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought [as you have described], I would not be named Subhūti; I would be one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
*Araṇā* translates into Chinese as “non-contention” (*wúzhēng*). Subhūti said:

“If I were to harbor such a thought while seeking this path, I would then be not free from desire and would possess a mind of contention. Thus, the Buddha would not [recognize me] among his disciples.”
Among them, he alone specifically praised Subhūti as one who delights in the practice of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*).

He thought, "Though I have practiced this all day long, in truth, I have no mind that has attained this practice of non-contention. Therefore, the World-Honored One bestowed upon me the name Subhūti, saying, "This one is a practitioner who delights in *araṇā*.
This is why he declared me to be the foremost; it was because I had no such [deliberate] mind.
If attaining the fruit is thus, then those who have attained the four fruits do so without the mind’s acquisition; is this not a further cause for faith? Fu’s eulogy says:

"Where there is no birth, there is no extinction; where there is no self, there is likewise no person. The obstacles of affliction are forever eliminated, and one takes long leave of future existence.
When objects are forgotten, the mind also ceases; greed and anger no longer arise. Without compassion yet possessing empty wisdom, one is carefree."
"Truly relying on the One. Master Chuan said, "If you recognize it, as before, it is not so. The verse says: A bright pearl is hidden within the oyster’s belly;
Jade is concealed within the rock. A musk deer naturally possesses its fragrance; Why must it stand in the wind?
When one examines their livelihood, it seems as if there is nothing at all; Yet in every application, everything is fully present.
Chapter Ten: Adorning the Pure Land. This is the adornment of the pure ground of the mind.
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? [and so on] until: "In reality, there is nothing to be obtained in the Dharma."
Dīpaṃkara Buddha is none other than Dīpaṅkara Buddha. At the time of his birth, the radiance of his body was like a lamp; later, upon attaining Buddhahood, he was thus named Dīpaṃkara.

He was the teacher who bestowed the prophecy upon Śākyamuni Buddha. Although it was stated above that one attains the fruit of Buddhahood without a mind, in reality, the word "attainment" has never been absent;
ultimately, it still clings to a trace of conceptual form. Therefore, the Buddha asked: "In the past, I..."
"While listening to the Dharma in the presence of our Teacher, did you gain anything from that Dharma? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One.

Although the Tathāgata was taught by the Teacher while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, it was because his own nature is fundamentally pure, inherently free from defilement, and eternally luminous in its stillness. He awakened to Buddhahood; truly, it was not [attained] from the teacher."
It is attained by abiding in hearing and learning. If there were anything attained, how could one avoid the burden of having a mind?
Fu Song said: "In the past he was called Shanhui; today he is named Nengren. Observe conditions—they are but delusions; observe the essence of consciousness—it is not truly real.
The nature of dharmas is neither cause nor effect; suchness does not follow from causes. To say that he received the prediction of Dīpaṃkara—how could one know?"
This is the old body.
Subhūti, what do you think? [From "up to"] it is not adornment; it is called adornment.
The Buddha-field is the bodhicitta. As for "adornment," it means that the mind is always pure, does not seek outwardly, and proceeds spontaneously.

To follow conditions is to have nothing to attain. To be in accord with the Way whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, and to be free from deluded thoughts—this is what is meant by universal purity.
Since I have attained nothing, I am externally untainted by the six sense objects and internally free from the burden of private desires and deviant thoughts.
Thus, regarding the timing of a Bodhisattva’s cultivation, how could one seek adornment with a deliberate mind?
Therefore, he asked Subhūti: "Does one who is a bodhisattva actually accomplish the adornment of Buddha-lands?
Subhūti replied: "No. Since their nature is like the great void, there is fundamentally nothing such as 'adornment.
To have the ground made of gold and forests of the seven treasures are all matters of external ornamentation; they are not true adornment. As for the midst of true nature,"
The six perfections and the myriad practices—including all wholesome dharmas such as generosity, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are all forms of adornment.
However, one must not allow them to be intermingled with deluded thoughts; otherwise, they are merely empty names of adornment.
How could one have a mind that seeks after them? Fu’s verse says: "To sweep clean the ground of the mind is called the cause of the Pure Land."
Whether regarding merit or wisdom, first abandon greed and anger. Adorned with the transcendence of subject and object, there is neither self nor person.
Severing all without defilement, one emerges from the clamor of the world like a sharp blade. Master Chuanshan said: "The trousers born of one's mother."
The Lin-chi Record: The Blue-Green Province Cloth Shirt. The verse says: Shaking off his entire body, it is whiter than frost; the reed flowers, snow, and moon vie with one another for brilliance.
Fortunately, he possesses the posture of one poised to leap from the Ninefold Heights; what harm is there in adding a crimson crest?
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [up to] should give rise to their mind without dwelling on anything.
The Buddha said: "The mind cannot be known to adorn buddha-fields. Therefore, you practitioners who cultivate the path..."
One should know that this mind is eternally empty and quiescent by nature, devoid of all delusive thoughts, neither arising nor ceasing, unmoving and unshakable;
being thus pure, those who cultivate the six perfections and the myriad practices should give rise to such a pure mind.

One should not give rise to the mind through attachment to anything. If one gives rise to the mind by dwelling in attachment to the six sense objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—it is not pure.
Ordinary beings, through the arising and ceasing of ignorance, engage in deluded and inverted thoughts, grasping at and rejecting views concerning the noble and the ordinary, or good and evil;
this is called a turbid and disturbed mind, which arises because of contact with external objects.
Thus, the mind arises, like a monkey grasping at the moon or a person with diseased eyes seeing flowers. All phenomena arise from the mind;
wherever the mind dwells, that is deluded thought. The six sense objects compete to arise, like drifting clouds, coming and going without fixed stability.
If one awakens to true emptiness, there is no place for it to dwell, which is itself wisdom; thus, all afflictions cease to exist.
It can be seen that those bodhisattvas who wish to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—how could they possibly give rise to a mind that dwells with attachment to the six sense objects?
They should instead give rise to their minds in a state of non-attachment;
thus, this mind will arise spontaneously and irresistibly as the single, untainted mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*). How could it be otherwise?
It is not impure. Since it is called "pure," what kind of adornment is there? It is like a balance scale: when there is nothing in the pan, its heart is naturally upright.
When one utters the single word "birth" (*janman*), one immediately perceives that although the Buddha-dharma is profound, it is without marks (*animitta*).
How could it ever teach people to become like parched wood or extinguished ashes? Master Chuan said: "Even though it is thus, what can one do about what is before one's eyes? (Verse follows).
It is said: "Seeing form is not a matter of form; hearing sound is not a matter of sound. In the place where form and sound do not obstruct, one personally arrives at the City of the Dharma King.
It is also said: "Step back, step back! Look, look! Even the stubborn rock moves. A verse says:
"Sitting silently in the mountain hall on a quiet night, the profound stillness and vast emptiness are fundamentally natural. When will the western wind stir the forests and wilds? One..."
The sound is like the cry of a cold wild goose echoing across the vast sky.
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person... [as stated by the Buddha] "that which is not a body is called a great body.
This metaphor illustrates the greatness of the mind. The human mind can give rise to ten thousand transformations and changes; since all things emerge from it, it is so named.
Therefore, it is compared to Sumeru, the King of Mountains. Sumeru is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li* in height and breadth.
The sun and moon revolve around the mountain, creating day and night. From this, its four sides are divided into the four continents (*cāturdvīpa*).
Above it lies the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). It may be called the most vast, the king of all mountains. [People...]
How could the body truly possess such greatness? The Buddha taught that the human mind fills the six voids and dwells in purity;
this is truly sufficient to fill heaven and earth and span past and present. It is by entrusting this [mind] to a name that it is called the "Great Body," not because there is actually a Great Body.
People do not seek it in purity, but instead seek possession and seek to obtain adornment.
Does the Mother, in turn, look down upon its mind as something small? Master Chuans said: "Even if there were one, where would you place it? He offered this verse:

"If you intend to take Mount Sumeru and make it a phantom body, Though your gall may be large and your heart coarse, I point out before your eyes that of the thousand kinds of 'self,' Not even one among them exists. Enter right here. Master Fu’s verse says: "Sumeru..."
High and vast, it serves as a metaphor for the body of the Dharma King. The seven treasures encircle it in equal measure, and the six perfections stand side by side in succession.

Formed from the four colors, it takes on the appearance of a mountain; compassion acts as the cause for Buddhahood. That which has form can never be truly great; only that which is signless is the ultimate reality.
Chapter Eleven: The Superiority of Merit from Non-action. To uphold this sutra and deliver others requires no artificial effort;
such merit is most supreme.
Subhūti, as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges River—let alone those sands themselves—are already countless and immeasurable. How much more so the merit of one who upholds this sutra!
In the western lands there is a river called the Ganges, forty *li* in circumference, situated near the place where the Buddha preached the Dharma;
for this reason, the Buddha took it as a metaphor. The sand of the Ganges is exceedingly fine and abundant. Take a single grain of that sand...
Compared to a single river, there are immeasurable Ganges Rivers;
if one were to take all the grains of sand within those immeasurable Ganges Rivers and calculate them as a whole, they would be exceedingly numerous and inexhaustible. Therefore, Subhūti said:
"If even the Ganges Rivers themselves are so extremely many as to be beyond calculation, how much more so the sands within them? Master Chuan said: "The former..."
Three threes; then three threes again. The verse says: One, two, three, four—counting as many as the sands of the Ganges; even more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.
When one has calculated until not a single dharma remains before the eyes, only then can one abide in stillness: *sārvaha*.
"Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth" (up to) "this merit surpasses the previous merit.
"In truth" means that the words are not false or erroneous; it is intended for people to believe.

Taking the sands within all those rivers, and calculating one three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system for every single grain of sand—this is an extreme description of the vast number of world-systems. To receive [them]...
Holding even a single four-line verse, though it may not equal the merit of giving away the seven treasures, truly gives rise to the wisdom-mind within me.
Furthermore, if one can explain it to others, then everyone will together attain the fruit of Buddhahood and accomplish the Unsurpassed Way;
therefore, the resulting reward of merit is far superior to that of material giving. It is evident that one must certainly uphold the sutras.

When explaining this for others, some may say that giving (dāna) is the foremost of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). They claim that the merit derived from such giving does not equal that of one who upholds this sutra.
Why is this? It is because although one may give the seven treasures without any stinginess, it is only when one actually possesses those seven treasures that one’s intention can be fulfilled.
If one lacks the seven treasures, one cannot practice giving. Furthermore, one must understand that although the seven treasures...
Much, yet it does not exceed the limited things of the human realm. To give with these is merely to receive limited human merit.
Material giving is exhaustible; the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible. Material giving does not transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
the gift of Dharma can transcend the three realms (*tridhātu*). If one receives and upholds the principles within this sutra, then one will not—
Bound by evil karma, one may thereby awaken to and clarify the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, by explaining it to others, one enables them also to hear this ultimate principle and together clarify the true nature. After a long time, when the roots of goodness have all matured, one can escape saṃsāra and forever transcend birth and death.
This is the way of delivering people through upholding the sutra; whether in poverty or in prosperity, day after day, it is possible.
It can be practiced daily; it can be practiced everywhere. It is inexhaustible and boundless. How vast is such merit! Zen Master Zhizhe composed a verse on this:
"The number of Ganges Rivers is already immense, yet the number of their sands is even more difficult to measure. If one were to take all these sands and match them with the seven treasures..."
One may be able to uphold the nectar of wisdom, yet all that possesses form is but an illusion; to speak merely of the power of wisdom is in vain.
Were one to discuss even a single four-line verse, this merit would not be considered great. Master Chuan said: "Brass cannot be exchanged for gold. The verse says:

Entering the sea to count the sands is but a waste of effort; such petty toil cannot avoid the dust of the mundane world. How could it compare to bringing forth the treasure from within one's own home?
Flowers blooming on withered wood—a spring of a different sort.
○ Section Twelve: Honoring the Orthodox Teaching. The Buddha’s teaching is great and correct; those who receive and uphold it will inspire respect and reverence from both devas and humans.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whoever explains this sutra (up to the point where it says) "they should all be honored as if they were stupas or shrines of the Buddha.
Subhūti, having engaged in detailed analysis with the Buddha, did not dare to sit at ease to receive the teaching;
therefore, the Buddha again commanded him to take his place and told him: "When explaining it for others, there is no need for discrimination; wherever [it may be]..."
Wherever one sees people and immediately expounds this sutra with a mind free from discrimination— even if it be only as few as four lines of verse—
one should know that such a place where the sutra is preached is itself the site where the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma.
It causes all listeners to give rise to a pure mind, free from all delusive thoughts, and to awaken to their original Buddha-nature.
This very illusory body is the Dharma-body; within it lies the complete *śarīra* of the Tathāgata.
It moves the deities of heaven and the people of the world, as well as the evil classes among the eight divisions of spirits, such as the Asuras, all [to pay homage].

One should respectfully make offerings with flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, streamers, canopies, fragrant oils, and ghee lamps, treating it as one would a stupa containing the relics of the Buddha’s physical remains.
One should establish a temple for this extraordinary image of the Buddha. The verse states:
With the sands of the Ganges as its measure, it is divided into six kinds of abundance. To uphold this sutra and grasp even four lines of verse—how could the seven treasures ever surpass this?

This gateway of Dharma is the place where one wanders; through making offerings here, one inspires the asuras. Within the sutras, it is called the most supreme; its majesty and loftiness are like those of a Buddha.

How much more so for a person who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra]—even down to a single four-line verse from within this scripture—staying in this place and preaching it; such a person would still be able to move the heavens.
How much more so for a person who is able to fully uphold and recite the entire sutra? You should know that the dharma accomplished by such a person is...
This is the most supreme, foremost, and rare Dharma. How could it not evoke even greater reverence from devas, humans, and others?
Such is the wondrous power of the scriptures’ resonance and penetration. Thus we know that wherever the sutras are present, the Buddha himself is present there;
it is as if the Buddha, together with his disciples and bodhisattvas, is all gathered in that place. If a person sees the sutras, then...
Having personally seen the Buddha, how could one not maintain the recitation and expound it?

If an ordinary person can recite this sutra from their own mind, understand its meaning from their own mind, and realize within their own mind the principle of signlessness and non-attachment, wherever they may be—
Constantly cultivate the practices of the Buddha, with every thought-moment uninterrupted.

When the mind is ever-pure, neither arising nor ceasing, and free from all delusive thoughts, one may immediately attain Buddhahood upon this very ground. Thus, one sees that the mind itself is the Buddha;
therefore it is said that wherever one is, there is a Buddha. "Venerable disciples" refers to those such as Bodhisattvas who are able to realize the wondrous state of formlessness.
The principle is indeed worthy of respect. Master Chuan said, "It should be thus. The verse says: As deep as the ocean, as firm as a mountain;
turning left and turning right, neither departing nor abiding. A golden-maned lion cub emerging from its den.

With full majesty he roars, dispelling all doubts; deep contemplation remains unmoved in the realm where weapons are absent. He directly gathers the celestial Māras and those of external paths back into the fold.
Master Gaofeng’s verse says: "The mind itself is Buddha; there is no other dharma. Those who are deluded seek it outside the mind.
In a single thought, vast and open, one returns to the fundamental limit—just like washing one's feet and stepping onto the bow of a boat. A monk asked the Master Shou...
A mountain. [A monk asked: "What is the Buddha? The Mountain replied: "The daughter-in-law rides the donkey; the mother-in-law leads it.
Chan Master Gushan Gui composed a verse on this: Mother-in-law and daughter-in-law share the same path; The hometown is but a short distance away.
How laughable are those who ride a donkey seeking a donkey; Their whole lives they mistake the saddle-bridge for their home.
Chapter Thirteen: Receiving and Upholding According to the Dharma. Relying upon the Dharma as taught by the Buddha, one receives it and maintains it.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One... [up to] ...this is called the Prajñāpāramitā.”
Subhūti, seeing that the Tathāgata had praised this sūtra, requested its name so that he and the others might honor and uphold it.
The Buddha said: "Those who understand this sūtra possess wisdom as sharp and resilient as the diamond of gold;
they are able to sever all things characterized by signs and eliminate all false delusions."
This thought leads directly to the other shore of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; it is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should honor and uphold it. It resides solely within your own mind, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Do not allow for conceptual discrimination; you will then be able to sever all doubts and attachments. However, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is emptiness itself;

one must not grasp at this as a characteristic. Upon awakening to and clarifying the fundamental nature, it is as tranquil as the great void. Since even its substance does not exist, how could there be a name for it?

The Tathāgata feared that people might give rise to the view of annihilationism; having no choice but to provisionally establish these names, he gave the empty designation "Prajñāpāramitā" in order to guide sentient beings.
As he taught, he simultaneously swept away his own words, fearing only that people would dwell upon signs (*nimitta*).
Master Guizong said: "A lecturer came to visit him while Guizong was weeding. Seeing a..."
A snake appeared. [Zhao] cut it in half. The Master said, "I have long looked up to Guizong; it turns out he is but a monk of coarse conduct.
Guizong said, "Is it you who are coarse, or am I who am coarse? Tell me, where does this monk’s fault lie? Chan Master Zhao composed a verse for him, saying:
"The Master of Mount Lu received those of superior capacity; He cut the snake, manifesting compassion in a special way. The deluded ones sit in confusion..."
The Master was struck with alarm and said, "It is carelessness that invites trouble.
Subhūti, what do you think? [He] addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has taught nothing."
The fundamental mind is originally pure; all phenomena are originally empty. What further dharma could there be to speak of?

Those of the Two Vehicles cling to the notion that persons and dharmas exist, and thus they have something to say. The Bodhisattva, having realized that both persons and dharmas are empty, has nothing to say.
The Buddha has merely provisionally named this "Vajracchedikā Prajñāpātra Sūtra," yet he has never truly pointed out within the sūtra itself, saying, "This is it."
"What kind of dharma could possibly possess a truly existent *prajñāpāramitā*? Hanshanzi said:
"My mind is like the autumn moon, Its light shining brightly upon the azure pool. Nothing can be compared to it; How am I to describe it? Chuan Chan Master said:
"Lower your voice! Lower your voice! He then offered this verse: "Entering the grass to seek the person—what can be done? The sharp blade..."
The sword severs the hand, yet it is rubbed and smoothed; though there is no trace of its coming or going, is the full manifestation of its patterns not seen?
Subhūti, what do you think? From "the three thousand great thousand [worlds]" to "it is not a world, it is called a world."
How can it be seen that the Dharma is ineffable? This present trichiliocosm is formed through immeasurable causes and conditions.
How could all sentient beings exist apart from this world? Those who have awakened dwell within it; those who are deluded likewise dwell within it.
The mind of the awakened one is the pure mind. It is with this mind that one dwells in this world.
This is precisely the world of purity. It is the mind of the deluded, a mind defiled by dust and grime.
When this mind dwells in this world, it becomes a world of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). While the worlds are many, the subtle particles are even more numerous than that.
If all sentient beings were to give rise to a pure mind, they could not be defiled by these subtle particles; therefore, it is said: "not by subtle particles."
Dust. Having attained the supramundane Dharma, it cannot be interrupted by the world; therefore, it is called "non-world.
Abiding in the world yet detached from the world, abiding in dust yet detached from dust—it can be seen that there is truly no fixed form of even a single mote of dust.
It is merely a false name for "dust. When the Tathāgata speaks of the world, there is likewise no fixed form of a real world.
Furthermore, all mountain cliffs will eventually crumble and split; all rivers and streams will eventually dry up.

It is merely a false name that we call "the world. If one insists on saying that the Buddha possesses a dharma, then it would follow that atoms truly exist as atoms and the world truly exists as a world.
